paragraphs.text: For many environmentalists, the world seems to be getting warmer. As one of the countries nearest to the South Polar Region, New Zealand has maintained an upward trend in its average temperature in the past few years. However, the temperature in New Zealand will go up 4°C in the next century while the polar region will go up more than 6°C. New Zealand’s lower projected increase is due to the surrounding ocean, which acts like an air conditioner. Thus New Zealand is comparatively fortunate.

Scientifically speaking, this temperature phenomenon in New Zealand is associated with what researchers call “SAM” (Southern Annular Mode), which refers to the wind belt that circles the Southern Ocean around New Zealand and Antarctica. Yet recent work has revealed that changes in SAM in New Zealand have resulted in a reduction in the moisture carried by winds during summer, and more rainfall in other seasons. A bigger problem may turn out to be more severe agricultural droughts, as increased water loss from the soil results in poorer harvests when winter rainfall arrives too late to save them.

Among all the problems caused by drought, moisture deficit is the most serious. Moisture deficit is the gap between the water plants need during the growing season and the water available from the soil. Measures of moisture deficit were at their highest since the 1970s in New Zealand. Meanwhile, ecological analyses clearly show that moisture deficit has different effects at different stages of crop growth. If moisture deficit occurs around a crucial growth stage, it will reduce grain yield by about 22 per cent compared with a deficit during the vegetative phase.

Global warming is not only affecting agricultural production. When scientists say the country’s snowpack and glaciers are melting at an alarming rate due to global warming, this places additional strain on local areas. For example, when global warming is accompanied by a rising snow line, the local skiing industry faces a crisis. The snow line may move up as the temperature goes up, and then the snow at the bottom will melt earlier. Fortunately, increased snowfall in some areas may help the local skiing industry through difficult periods.

How do glacier regions respond? Climate change is reflected in the glacier regions of southern New Zealand, where land is covered by ice and snow. The reaction of a glacier to a climatic change involves a complex chain of processes. Over periods ranging from years to several decades, cumulative changes in mass balance cause volume and thickness changes, which affect the flow of ice via altered internal deformation and basal sliding. This dynamic response finally leads to changes in glacier length—that is, the advance or retreat of glacier tongues. Undoubtedly, glacier mass balance is a more direct signal of annual atmospheric conditions.

The latest research from the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research (NIWA) shows that the glacier line keeps moving up because of the impacts of global warming. Further ice loss is evident in the Mount Cook region. By 1996, a 14-km-long sector of the glacier had melted, forming a melt lake (Hooker Lake). Melting of the glacier front at a rate of 40 m per year will cause the glacier to retreat at a rather uniform rate. Therefore, the lake will continue to grow until it reaches the glacier bed.

A direct result of melting glaciers is a change in high tides, which is a major factor in sea-level rise. The trend of rising sea levels threatens the groundwater system by making groundwater hypersaline and may then reduce agricultural production. Many experts believe that the best way to counter this trend is to take a longer-term view of sea-level change in New Zealand. Indeed, the coastal boundaries need to be upgraded and redefined.

There is no doubt that global warming has affected New Zealand in many aspects. The response to global warming should be based on the joint efforts of local people and experts to address difficult conditions. For instance, farmers are taking a long-term, multigenerational approach to adjust breeds and species to changing temperatures. Agriculturists also find ways to tackle the problems climate change may cause for the soil. In broad terms, going forward, the ecosystem’s long-established resilience is expected to continue.

How about animals’ responses? Experts have found that animals can adapt to global warming in unusual ways. A study has examined sea turtles on a few northern beaches in New Zealand and found that sea turtles become male or female depending on the nest temperature. Further research will try to find out how rising temperatures affect their sex ratio. Clearly, the temperature of the nest determines the sex of hatchlings.

Tackling the problems of global warming is never easy in New Zealand, because records show that the slow process of global warming may have different impacts on various regions. New Zealand accounts for only 0.5 per cent of the world’s carbon dioxide emissions, and its emissions meet government standards.
However, New Zealand’s efforts are only the tip of the iceberg. So far, global warming remains a global issue with an uncertain future.

questionGroups.text:
Questions 27–32
Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 27–32 on your answer sheet.


27 What is the main idea of the first paragraph?
 A The temperature in the polar region will increase less than that in New Zealand in the next
   century.
 B New Zealand’s weather and climate are very important to its people because of its close
   location to the polar region.
 C New Zealand will maintain high air quality because of the ocean.
 D New Zealand’s temperature will increase less than that of other regions in the next 100
   years because it is surrounded by sea


28 What is one effect of the wind belt that circles the Southern Ocean?
 A New Zealand’s winds will contain more moisture in summer.
 B New Zealand will face droughts more often in the hotter months of the year.
 C Soil moisture will increase as the winds become drier.
 D Agricultural production will be reduced as a result of more rainfall in other seasons


29 What does “moisture deficit” mean for grain and crops?
 A Growing conditions will be very difficult for crops.
 B The growing season of some plants can hardly be determined.
 C There will be a huge gap between the water plants need and the water available from the
   soil.
 D The soil supporting grain and crops in New Zealand recorded its lowest productivity since
   the 1970s.


30 What changes will happen to the skiing industry due to the global warming phenomenon?
 A A ski resort may lower its skiing altitude.
 B Some ski resorts may need to move north.
 C Snowfall may increase at some ski resorts.
 D Local ski resorts may make a profit because of the snowfall increase.

31 Cumulative changes over a long period of time in mass balance will lead to
 A Alterations in the volume and thickness of glaciers.
 B Faster changes in internal deformation and basal sliding.
 C An increase in the length of glaciers.
 D Retreat of glacier tongues as a result of change in annual atmospheric conditions.


32 Why does the writer mention NIWA in the sixth paragraph?
 A To use a particular example to explain the effects of glacier melting.
 B To emphasize the severity of further ice loss in the Mount Cook region.
 C To alert the reader to the uniform rate at which glaciers are melting.
 D To note that the lake in the region will disappear when it reaches the glacier bed.

Questions 33–35
Complete the summary below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 33–35 on your answer sheet.


Research data show that sea level has a close relationship with climate
change. The major reason for the increase in sea level is connected with 33
_________________. The rise in sea level also threatens the groundwater
system; its destruction may lead to a reduction in 34 _________________.
In the long run, New Zealand may have to upgrade its 35
_________________ to reduce the effects of changing sea levels.

Questions 36–40
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet write
 YES                      if the statement agrees with the views of the writer

 NO                       if the statement contradicts the views of the writer

 NOT GIVEN                if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this


36 _________________ Farmers respond less to climate change than agricultural experts do.
37 _________________ The agricultural sector is too conservative and resistant to dealing with

38 _________________ Sea turtles are vulnerable to climate change.
39 _________________ Global warming is progressing slowly, and it may have different effects
